title: Forest dwellers and fisher workers
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The Vanawasi Gramin and Mathsya federations.
body:
Among the less well-known federations of Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) are the **Akhil Bharatiya Vanawasi Gramin Mazdoor Mahasangh**, which works among forest-dwelling workers, and the **Akhil Bharatiya Mathsya Mazdoor Mahasangh**, which works among fisheries workers. Both appear on the list of 38 federations on the BMS website. They are not names that appear daily in the news, and the people they represent rarely figure in the statistics that shape labour policy. This post looks at the law and the schemes that touch their lives, the problems each group faces, and why BMS keeps them in its structure.

## Forest-dwelling workers

Communities who live in and near forests depend on a mixture of activities. They collect **minor forest produce**, such as honey, tendu leaves and other items that are not timber; they work as labourers in forest operations; and they cultivate small plots, often without a clear paper title. Much of their income is seasonal and much of it passes through traders, which means the person who climbs the tree or walks the forest path usually receives only a small part of the final price.

The central law for these communities is the **Forest Rights Act, 2006**. It recognises the rights of Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers over forest land and forest produce. Under the Act, a non-tribal claimant must show that the family has depended on forest land for at least three generations before 13 December 2005. The Act places weight on women's names in individual and community claims. It is implemented by State governments, which receive claims, verify them through village-level processes and issue titles.

How far has implementation gone? A reply by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs in the Rajya Sabha, reported with data as of 30 June 2022, gave the following picture:

- About 44.46 lakh claims had been received, of which about 42.77 lakh were individual and about 1.69 lakh were community claims.
- About 22.36 lakh titles had been distributed, about 21.33 lakh individual and about 1.03 lakh community, covering about 1.60 crore acres of forest land.
- Community titles covered most of the land recognised, because each community title covers a large area.
- The data covered only some States and Union Territories, and it did not report how many claims were rejected or why.

The numbers show that a large share of claims received did not end in a title, and it is the unexplained gap that concerns forest-dweller organisations. Claims can be rejected for want of documents that a forest family never had; they can stay pending for years; and recognised titles are not always marked on the land records. Community rights over forest produce are weaker in practice than on paper if the village does not know how to use them. These are matters of administration more than of law, and they depend heavily on how each State carries out its task.

The Ministry of Tribal Affairs also runs schemes aimed at giving forest produce collectors a better price, including support prices for selected minor forest produce and Van Dhan centres where collectors can add value to produce locally. Readers who want current details of those schemes should consult the Ministry's pages, since coverage and rates are revised from time to time.

The concerns the federation raises can be put simply: **recognition of claims**, **fair prices** for what is collected, **wages and safety** for forest labour, and **protection against displacement** when land is diverted for other uses.

## Fisheries workers

India's fishing communities work in the sea and in inland waters, from small boats off the coast to rivers, reservoirs and ponds. The Government's own scheme documents recognise the sector as a source of livelihood for a very large number of people. The main Central scheme is the **Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY)**, launched in 2020-21, which the Fisheries Minister has described in Parliament as an investment of about Rs 20,990.79 crore across all States and Union Territories. It deals with fisheries infrastructure, fish production, fishers' incomes and social security.

For workers, one part of it is of particular interest, the **Group Accidental Insurance Scheme**. It gives marine and inland fishers and allied fish workers Rs 5 lakh for death or permanent total disability from an accident, Rs 2.5 lakh for permanent partial disability, and up to Rs 25,000 towards hospitalisation for accidental injury. The premium is shared between the Centre and the States, most often in a 60:40 ratio, with a larger Central share for Himalayan and North-Eastern States and full payment for Union Territories. The Minister told the Rajya Sabha in August 2024 that about 131.3 lakh fishermen were covered under the insurance scheme. In addition, fishers and fish farmers have been eligible for the **Kisan Credit Card** since 2018-19, to meet working capital needs through formal credit.

The problems that fishing workers describe go beyond what insurance can solve.

- **Declining catch and rising costs.** Fuel is a large part of the cost of going to sea, and a poor season can mean a loss.
- **Competition among fishing methods and regulation of zones.** Traditional boats, mechanised boats and larger vessels share the same waters, and rules on zones and seasons are a source of dispute.
- **Weak social security.** Insurance for accidents is helpful, but fishers also need health cover, pension and income support for the months when fishing is banned or the weather is bad.
- **Cyclone and weather risk.** Storms are a danger to life and boats, and timely, understandable warnings are a matter of survival.
- **Shore-side workers.** Women who sort, dry and sell fish, and those who work in processing, deserve equal attention in schemes and statistics.

## The common point

Both groups live and work at the edge of the formal economy. They are rarely employed under written contracts, they work in places far from labour offices, and their earnings depend on nature and on traders. Labour statistics usually count them only partly. A federation structure matters in such a case, because it gives a national voice to groups that would otherwise be heard only in their own district.

BMS includes them so that their issues reach the national agenda, and the labour codes show why this is needed. The Code on Social Security covers unorganised workers and provides for schemes to be notified for them, yet the usefulness of a scheme depends on whether a forest collector or a fisher knows about it, is registered and can claim without a long journey. Registration on the e-Shram portal, awareness drives in villages and coastal hamlets, and simple claim procedures are the practical tools.

## What remains to be done

For forest-dwelling workers, the next steps are speedy and transparent disposal of pending Forest Rights Act claims with reasons given for rejection, recording of titles in land records, and better price realisation for forest produce. For fisheries workers, they are wider health and pension cover, support during ban seasons, reliable cyclone warnings in local languages and better recognition of women in the fish economy. For both, the common need is accurate data, so that planners can see the workers they are planning for.

## What you can do

When you buy fish, or forest produce such as honey and tendu-leaf products, ask how much of the price reaches the person who collected it. The question is a simple way of connecting a shopping basket with a livelihood.
